prompt: Why does the symmetric C=C stretch of (E)-2-butene (CH₃CH=CHCH₃) NOT appear in the IR?

options.label: The symmetric stretch produces no net dipole-moment change, so the vibration is IR-inactive
The C=C bond is too strong — its stretching frequency falls above the IR window
The vibration is at a frequency outside the typical IR scanning range (above 4000 cm⁻¹)
The C=C stretch is degenerate with the C-C single bond stretches, so the peaks cancel

explanation: The IR selection rule: a vibration must cause a dipole-moment change to absorb. In (E)-2-butene the two methyls move symmetrically outward — the dipole doesn't change. The vibration happens, it just can't absorb IR light. Terminal and unsymmetric alkenes DO show C=C around 1640.
